chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
title: Billy Fowler's Monte Carlo band and learning from Henry Walton
summary: Billy Fowler's professional dance band, newly back from Monte Carlo, was Butler's first big band of pros; trumpeter Henry Walton taught him wisdom if tersely.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: So this man Billy Fowell, he just had come back from

Monte Carlo. A lot of people going various places, so he had come back from Monte Carlo and he was organizing a band. I was in the band, and we had violins, singers, and everyone singing (inaudible). And had a trumpet player -- I forget his last name. Oscar, I know. And I always liked to play with people, and he liked me. I was hauling that man, (inaudible) and now thinking that that man hadn't liked me, I had to stop that immediate because he was very, very conservative, man. You know, it was a dance band and you would play and say nothing to nobody, but he knew his instrument. And I was learning from him, too.

Well, then, this is my first feeling of a big band with pro's, everybody was a pro. You have records behind/I played so and so, I played here and there. The fellow on the guitar, his name was Edward Gibbs. He was young, we were all sort of younger people. The key men were older people. And Henry Walton, I learned so much from him. Wisdom.
He played trumpet. He had a beautiful velvet sound. He was just amazing, between Oscar and Walton, I was asking Walton questions and he wouldn't answer.
That annoyed me. He says, 'Well, I heard you.' And then he would say (inaudible) and that was all I could get. But I remember to this day, it was beauti-
ful. That was his way. But he knew the horn.
Would you be asking musical questions?

Musical. I'd ask him various questions of this. And he said, I've lived in Europe, I've lived in (inaudible). He'd explain it to me. And then if I wouldn't ask him no more, I wouldn't get no more. But I was there everyday, beggin him, or as we said bugging him, but I was learning. I was a little bit dumb so that was why I was asking questions. I didn't want to stay dumb.
